s50m:S1Q04F.q: How would you reduce the sorting cost for millions of customers while preserving the tie rule?
s50m:S1Q04F.label: gemini-3.1-flash-lite_fturn-s50m-B
s50m:S1Q04F.spoken: I’d use a partial sort with numpy.argpartition to isolate the top K elements in linear time, then perform a full sort only on that small subset. To handle the tie-breaking, I’d augment the scores with the negative row index before partitioning. This keeps the performance cost close to linear while guaranteeing the original order for ties.

s50m:S1Q06F.q: How would you index those tables, and what changes if historical records can be corrected after ingestion?
s50m:S1Q06F.label: gemini-3.1-flash-lite_fturn-s50m-B
s50m:S1Q06F.spoken:
For the snapshots table, I’d index (customer_id, snapshot_time) to support the join and the point-in-time filter. On the events table, I’d use a composite index on (customer_id, event_time, ingested_at) to allow the database to quickly filter the thirty-day window and enforce the ingestion time constraint without a full scan.

If historical records can be corrected, the ingested_at column alone isn't enough to guarantee point-in-time consistency. I’d switch to a bi-temporal modeling approach, adding a valid_from and valid_to timestamp to the events. This lets me query the state of the world exactly as it appeared at the snapshot time, even if the underlying data was updated later, by filtering for records where the snapshot time falls within the validity interval.

s50m:S2Q05F.q: Construct an example where that greedy policy gives poor coverage, and tell me how you would incorporate redundancy or multi hop dependence
s50m:S2Q05F.label: gemini-3.1-flash-lite_fturn-s50m-B
s50m:S2Q05F.spoken:
The greedy policy fails when the top results are clustered around a single sub-topic. For example, if I query "Compare 2023 and 2024 revenue," and the top five chunks are all from the 2023 annual report, I miss the 2024 data entirely, even if those chunks were highly relevant.

To fix this, I would implement Maximal Marginal Relevance, or MMR. It penalizes chunks that are semantically similar to ones already selected, forcing the system to prioritize novelty and coverage over raw relevance scores. For multi-hop dependencies, I’d use an agentic query decomposition approach, breaking the complex question into sub-queries and allocating a specific context budget for each hop to ensure the model has the right evidence for every step of the reasoning chain.

s50m:S2Q08F.q: How do you prove the replacement index is sufficiently complete and current before you send production traffic to it?
s50m:S2Q08F.label: gemini-3.1-flash-lite_fturn-s50m-B
s50m:S2Q08F.spoken: I validate completeness by running a checksum count against the source database to ensure every document ID exists in the new vector store. For currency, I run a shadow pipeline that mirrors live traffic to the new index, then use an LLM-as-judge evaluation suite to compare retrieval precision and recall against the current production index before the final cutover.
